N: Listen to a conversation between a student and an academic advisor.
Advisor: So, you're thinking about taking Introduction to Marketing next term?

Advisor: There is an online section, but it fills up quickly. If you want that one, you should register today.

Advisor: That makes sense. Still, the online section might be the better choice if your work schedule can't change.
Student: True. I'll call my manager this afternoon and see whether I can switch shifts. If not, I'll take the online class.

exercises.question: Why is the student worried about the course?
options: He has already failed it once.
He may not be free at the class time.
He thinks the teacher is too strict.

N: Listen to a public service announcement.
Announcer: This is a reminder for residents of North Park. Water service will be temporarily interrupted tonight from ten p.m. until approximately six a.m. while the city replaces an old underground pipe. Residents are advised to store enough water for drinking and basic cleaning before ten p.m. If possible, avoid using washing machines or dishwashers until service is fully restored in the morning. A supply tank with bottled water will be available at the North Park Community Center for elderly residents and others with urgent needs.
N: Now answer the questions.
exercises.question: Who is the bottled water especially intended for?
options: Residents with urgent needs, including older people
City workers on the night shift

exercises.audioText:
N: Listen to part of a podcast.
Host: When people feel stuck on a problem, they often assume they should stay at their desks and try harder. In fact, short walks can be surprisingly productive. Movement changes your environment and can interrupt repetitive thinking. One design team I interviewed now holds ten-minute walking meetings whenever they cannot agree on a solution. They say the conversations become calmer, and people tend to suggest more creative ideas. Of course, walking is not a replacement for focused work. You still need time to sit down, review options, and make a decision. But if your thinking starts to go in circles, getting up may be exactly what helps.
N: Now answer the questions.
exercises.question: What is the speaker's main point?
options: Good ideas only come from group discussions
Walking can help people think more effectively
Meetings should always take place outdoors
Designers are more creative than other workers
exercises.teacherNote: Target: Main Idea Comprehension. High potential for lapping in "Designers are more creative" if students only listen for keywords.

exercises.audioText: When the printing press spread across Europe in the fifteenth century, it did not just make books cheaper — it changed how information traveled entirely. Ideas that once took years to reach distant regions could now spread within months. This shift laid the groundwork for widespread literacy and, eventually, for public debate on a scale never seen before.
exercises.question: What is the main topic of this talk?
options: The impact of the printing press

N: Listen to a conversation in a university library.
Student: Hi, I need to renew a book, but I’ve already renewed it twice online.
Librarian: Yes, after two online renewals you have to bring the book in so we can check its condition.
Student: I have it here. I was hoping to keep it for another week because I’m finishing a research paper.
Librarian: Let me see. There’s no hold on it from other students, so I can renew it for seven more days. After that, though, you’ll need to return it.
Student: That’s perfect — my paper is due Friday.
N: Now answer the questions.
exercises.question: Why can’t the student renew the book online again?
options: He has already reached the online renewal limit.
exercises.explanation: After two online renewals the book must be brought in to check its condition.

exercises.audioText:
N: Listen to a manager talking to a team about a work policy.
Manager: As you know, we’re moving to a hybrid model next month. You’ll work from home Monday and Friday, and be in the office Tuesday through Thursday. The idea is to keep focused work at home but have in-person time for planning and training. Please update the shared calendar by this Friday so we know when to book meeting rooms. If you have concerns about equipment at home, talk to HR this week.
Team member: Will the office hours change?
Manager: No, hours stay nine to five, but you can request flexible start times through HR.
N: Now answer the questions.
exercises.question: When will employees work from home under the new model?
exercises.explanation: Manager says work from home Monday and Friday, in office Tuesday-Thursday.

exercises.audioText:
Woman: Your new book tackles the transition to renewable energy. Some critics argue your timeline of ten years is completely unrealistic given current infrastructure.
Man: I understand their skepticism. However, historical precedents—like the rapid industrialization in the 20th century—prove that when economic incentives align with political will, transitions happen exponentially faster than linear projections suggest.
exercises.ttsText: Your new book tackles the transition to renewable energy. Some critics argue your timeline of ten years is completely unrealistic given current infrastructure. I understand their skepticism. However, historical precedents—like the rapid industrialization in the 20th century—prove that when economic incentives align with political will, transitions happen exponentially faster than linear projections suggest.
exercises.question: How does the man defend his ten-year timeline?
options: By pointing out that the current infrastructure is already adequate.
By comparing it to fast shifts that occurred in the past.
By criticizing the economic incentives of fossil fuels.
By agreeing that his projections are purely theoretical.
exercises.explanation: He defends his timeline by citing 'historical precedents' (things that happened in the past) like 'rapid industrialization'.

When the renewal is done online
When it has been renewed twice

exercises.audioText: The university is introducing a shared bicycle program for students and staff. The first phase will include 120 bicycles at four locations near the main campus. Users will need to register online, and the first thirty minutes of each trip will be free. The university plans to evaluate the program after six months before deciding whether to expand it to the residential campus.
exercises.question: What will the university do after six months?
options: Evaluate the program before deciding about expansion
Move all bicycles to the residential campus
exercises.explanation: The university will evaluate the first phase before deciding whether to expand the program.
